title: I am looking for advice.
author: ChocolateTemporary48
selftext:
I’m working on my first serious game, created entirely using AI.

I have to admit that I have no programming experience; I’m doing this primarily because it’s an idea I’ve had for years.

To get straight to the point: I’m looking for advice on how to streamline my workflow, improve the visuals, and so on. If you have any tips or personal experiences to share, I’d love to hear them—it might also help others reading this post.

Right now, I’m using the Claude application with a €20/month subscription.

Following some advice, I’m essentially using Claude 3.5 Opus as a "lead" that directs "sub-agents" (Claude 3 Haiku) to carry out specific tasks; it then reviews their work and integrates it into the project.

Honestly, I’m not sure how sound this approach is.

As for the project itself, it’s a space-based 4X game. The concept is inspired by the UNSC versus the Covenant: an early-stage empire encounters a far superior civilization, and the player must use cunning and strategy to prolong the war and ultimately defeat the enemy.

replies.body:
I’m primarily looking to learn about people’s workflows—how you handle Claude’s limitations, manage prototypes, and work more efficiently with agents.

Also, what do you use for visuals? I’ve seen tools like Tripo or Blender MCP, but I’ve also seen people create them using code. I’d love some advice on the prompts I should be using or any other useful tools.

Essentially, I want to tap into the experiences of more seasoned users, rather than just fumbling around with Claude on my own.

replies.author: ChocolateTemporary48
replies.body:
My current concept is a 2D space-themed game—though a more complex one, inspired by \*Aurora 4X\* (which I highly recommend; it’s free).

The idea is a long-form campaign spanning 50 years or more, where you start off in a very poor position.

You’ll find yourself losing battle after battle, with only the occasional win. The core gameplay involves the player planning their technological development and construction efforts to contend with an enemy that is inherently superior—whether through a larger number of units, more advanced technology, or other such advantages.

The player must identify the enemy’s weaknesses and devise countermeasures—perhaps by pivoting toward a different technological path or by pouring all resources into industrial expansion.

That’s the general idea. Furthermore, the management aspect is quite involved: ships are detected via sensors, and weapons have varying ranges and speeds—that sort of thing.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
Don’t try to penny pinch too much. Haiku is going to give you garbage and structure with basic tasks. And context still needs to get passed even to lower agents so you’re not saving that much. Most of your work should be either opus calling sonnet or sonnet calling opus. 

More important is to track your context windows. Until your game is very large it’s a good idea to /compact and /clear often as it’s probably that much of your context will get eaten up by input. 

Art design doc early on is very important. It can also determine your platform, how you derive your assets etc the look and aesthetic you’re going for is very important to define. Otherwise you run a high risk of having a very bland pasted on asset look that most people would call ai slop

comments.author: arcarsenal986
comments.body:
I don't mean to sound like an asshole, but you can ask Claude, and it will give you a pretty honest breakdown of a good workflow. 

The best way to get good at this, is to just learn the workflow yourself over many months. People rag on AI being easy, its not an I WIN button. You do have to learn how to work with it.

replies.author: ChocolateTemporary48
replies.body: I understand what you’re saying. I actually asked Claude, but—as you know with LLMs—they tend to be overly focused on the prompt or take things too literally. That’s why I’m looking for advice; I’m hoping there might be some idea or topic that could be useful to me.

replies.author: arcarsenal986
replies.body:
And as someone else said, trying to force more agents can result in a bad outcome. Give it room to work, ask for a discussion on the workflow and the scope of the project, and it will make recommendations based on that information. 

Say you're open to use Blender, and Unity, or Godot. etc. You need to have an idea of what your game should look like to start, and then just iterate on it. You're going to want at least the $100 plan.

replies.author: ChocolateTemporary48
replies.body:
The problem is that my concept for the game is more complex than it should be, which significantly limits me in terms of visuals and mechanics.

I’m not sure if you’re familiar with \*Aurora 4X\*, but part of the inspiration came from there, along with other games like \*StarDrive\*.

On top of that, I’m still undecided about what art style to use; I know I can handle things like solar systems well, but I struggle more when it comes to ships and similar assets.

For now, I’m focusing on the mechanics. Once I have an alpha version, I’ll test it extensively to see what to add or remove, and only then will I focus on the visuals.

As for the €100 plan—I did consider it, honestly. But since this is more of a personal project and I highly doubt I’ll ever end up selling it, I don’t want to invest too much (not to mention that I don’t have many resources to begin with).

comments.author: magic-studios-admin
comments.body:
Latest advice is that the sub agent pattern doesn't really work with the latest models and leads to worse results. 

It's helpful to consider the different perspectives you maywant to bring to bear (uex, visuals, mechanics) but prompting the agent differently won't really result in better outcomes. 

Focus on understanding what good looks like and defining that explicitly for the agent but don't try to figure out how to tell the agent how to do the work. Modern models already know better than you if you give them a clear goal and something to compare against.

comments.author: Suecotero
comments.body:
Similar boat here: not a programmer, building a[ **strategy game**](https://www.reddit.com/r/TRAPPIST1/) (Godot 4 + C#) almost entirely with Claude, and learning to code as I go. Some things that actually made a difference for me:

**Workflow**

* Move from the chat app to Claude Code on a git repo as soon as you can. It reads and edits the whole project directly instead of you copy-pasting files around. Commit after every working change. When the AI breaks something (it will), you roll back instead of spending an evening arguing with it.
* Write a design doc first and keep it in the repo as a markdown file. Mine is a plain GDD covering the core loops, what the game is and isn’t, and the victory conditions. Point Claude at it at the start of every session. Most of the “it forgot what we decided” problems disappear.
* Your lead/sub-agent setup is fine in principle, but don’t over-engineer it. On a €20 plan the limits will bite long before the orchestration matters. Use the big model for planning and tricky systems and let the cheaper ones grind through routine stuff.
* Get to a playable loop with one objective as early as possible. Mine was “reach the first arcology.” A 4X has a frightening amount of surface area, and an ugly playable thing beats a beautiful design doc.
* Ask it to explain what it just did. Slowly, you start to recognise when it’s wrong.

**Visuals**

* Write an art brief before generating anything: reference games, palette, polycount target, camera distance. Mine is “Civ V/VI readability, hard-science industrial, off-white panels, graphite, restrained yellow accents, \~4k tris per unit.” Without it every asset looks like it came from a different game.
* Tripo’s Smart Mesh lets you set the face limit directly and exports GLB, which Godot takes as-is. Check the licence: on the free plan, models are published CC BY, and the licence is set when you generate them, not when you upgrade later.
* Blender MCP is great for cleanup (scale, pivot, orientation, export settings). For simple hard-surface stuff, Claude can model the thing directly in Blender. I got a six-wheeled rover at \~3.4k tris with baked AO, which is perfectly serviceable for a unit that’s a speck on a hex.
* Godot generates LODs on import by default, so don’t sweat polycounts too much. Textures cost more than triangles anyway.

Good luck. An underdog-vs-Covenant 4X is a good hook. 

Ok there's some advice, now time for [**shameless self-promo**:](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5423750/TRAPPIST1/)

comments.author: taisui
comments.body:
So here is the hard truth, turns out it's not that easy to make a good game regardless of the tooling.  I am already using Unity and I am a software engineer yet I find myself guiding Claude often on the most obvious things (it likes to take short cut doing what looks right but is not what I wanted).

Honestly the workflow is not magically the solution, the process takes iterations upon iterations, for someone without software experience you just have to find a process that works for you because my way of doing things is just way too complicated and will only be frustrating to you even more.

comments.author: Smashachuu
comments.body:
The idea is that you want to give the model a reference for what you're trying to recreate within your game. I hate doing this, but ask it to recreate a mechanic from the game that inspired the idea. It now has an entire Wikipedia page to reference for how the mechanics work within the game, what the triggers are etc.

Also, use design concepts that it generates to work from. For example, i'll ask for 10 UI designs as if 10 completely different people with different backgrounds and experiences had created them with their preferences in mind.  Then I'll have it cut those elements out and animate them into the UI.

Working backwards from a picture is 1000x better, because you gave it something to reference and iterate from. It has a visual to do list from that picture (I need to get the shadows to look like this, i need the shaders to have this hue and this vibe etc).

replies.author: ChocolateTemporary48
replies.body:
I provided Claude with several games as examples, along with the general concept, and we put together a plan covering mechanics and similar elements.

Once the prototype is complete, I’ll see what needs to be removed or adjusted.

I also suspect that one of the issues I’m facing now stems from the fact that I initially built the game’s foundation using ChatGPT (specifically version 6.1) before switching to Claude.

It’s possible that this may have limited me.

replies.author: Smashachuu
replies.body:
You could just import your history from codex to claude so it can gain insights into the skills. From my experience, claude is far more likely to change the request and continue generating it as if it was doing what you asked.  So instead of referecing a wikipedia page, it will try to reason how the mechanics work and get most of it wrong, spending 5x longer to give you a shitty request.

  
But it is faster.. You just have to babysit it far more.
